Two Revolutions from One Colloquium

GÖDEL, Kurt.; VON NEUMANN, John.

Ergebnisse eines mathematischen Kolloquiums, unter Mitwirkung von Kurt Gödel und Georg Nöbeling. Herausgegeben von Karl Menger. Heft 1–8.

Leipzig & Berlin: B.G. Teubner & F. Deuticke, 1931–1937. $35,000

First editions, a complete set of all eight Hefte in the original printed wrappers — the entire published record of Karl Menger’s Vienna Mathematical Colloquium, the alternate-Tuesday seminar that between 1928 and 1936 became the crucible of two distinct mathematical revolutions. To these slender wrappered pamphlets Kurt Gödel contributed fifteen papers and remarks on the foundations of logic and mathematics — among them the lecture in which he recast his incompleteness theorem in the form that became standard, and the short paper that reconciled classical with intuitionist arithmetic — while the last three Hefte carry the founding documents of modern mathematical economics, culminating in John von Neumann’s model of an expanding economy and the first existence proof for a competitive equilibrium. Complete runs are of the greatest rarity: no set of all eight has been traced through any major auction house in the past fifteen years, and the sets that do surface are almost always partial, wanting the scarce final Hefte. The colloquium met to pursue pure mathematics; it ended by reshaping two fields that had nothing obvious to do with one another.

Karl Menger (1902–85), a pupil of Hans Hahn, had taken his Vienna doctorate in 1924 and a professorship there in 1927 when, during the academic year 1928/29, several students asked him to direct a mathematical colloquium loosely modelled on the philosophically-minded Vienna Circle. It met on alternate Tuesdays in term, with a deliberately flexible agenda: lectures by members and invited guests, reports on recent publications, and the discussion of unsolved problems. Menger kept a record of the meetings and published it, by his own account each November of the following year, as the Ergebnisse eines mathematischen Kolloquiums, issued ‘unter Mitwirkung von Kurt Gödel und Georg Nöbeling’. Menger had first known Gödel as the youngest and most silent member of the Vienna Circle; Gödel began attending the colloquium in October 1929 and, after asking Menger to arrange his first meeting with the visiting Warsaw logician Alfred Tarski, soon took a hand in running it and editing its proceedings. He co-edited Hefte 2 to 5 and, after his 1933–34 year at the Institute for Advanced Study, Hefte 7 and 8 as well, confining his own spoken contributions, in the recollection of those present, to brief remarks stated with the greatest precision. The cast drawn to so modest a gathering was remarkable: Wald and Nöbeling among the regulars, Tarski and other Warsaw logicians as visitors, and von Neumann a contributor at a distance — affiliated, in one historian’s phrase, as a member in pectore — who would supply the last Heft its great economics paper. The enterprise did not so much conclude as disperse: Hahn died in 1934, Moritz Schlick was murdered by a former student in 1936, and Menger, disheartened by the situation in Austria, emigrated to the United States in 1937, where he revived the series in English as Reports of a Mathematical Colloquium (Notre Dame, 1939–48). The eight Vienna Hefte are the whole of the original.

What gave the colloquium its charge was the question then dominating foundations. David Hilbert had set mathematics the programme of securing itself once and for all — of proving, by strictly finitary means, that its formal systems are consistent and complete, so that every truth is provable and no contradiction can arise. Gödel had entered the university in 1924 and, working under Hahn, took the programme’s first question in his 1929 doctoral thesis, proving that first-order logic is complete: any valid formula can be derived from the axioms. Within two years he had answered the rest, and answered them in the negative. The incompleteness theorems showed that any sufficiently rich consistent system contains a true sentence it cannot prove, and that no such system can prove its own consistency from within — results that ended Hilbert’s programme as conceived and stand as the most consequential single contribution to twentieth-century mathematical logic. It is against this background that the contents of the present Hefte are read: Gödel worked out and announced much of the surrounding machinery here, in the proceedings of a seminar, in pieces of two and three pages. The colloquium was, in this sense, his working laboratory in the years of his greatest productivity, and the Hefte are the published trace of it — not selections made after the fact but the record as it was kept, week by week, with Gödel’s own hand on the editing.

Gödel’s fifteen contributions, catalogued in John Dawson’s annotated bibliography, fall across Hefte 2 to 5 and Heft 7. The weightiest is Über Vollständigkeit und Widerspruchsfreiheit (Heft 3, pp. 12–13), the lecture he gave to the colloquium’s twenty-fourth session on 22 January 1931 — the address required for his Habilitation, delivered while Menger was away in America and learned of only by letter. Months earlier Gödel had published the incompleteness theorem proper in Hahn’s Monatshefte, framed on the theory of types of Principia Mathematica; here he recast it on Peano’s axioms for the natural numbers and observed that any suitably axiomatised, ω-consistent system extending first-order arithmetic carries undecidable propositions. It was this version, built on arithmetic rather than type theory, that became the standard formulation, the one carried into the textbooks and into every later proof of the theorems. The seminar was also where the result’s significance was first weighed in person: Menger brought Oswald Veblen to hear Gödel speak, and Veblen, who had been primed by von Neumann, was sufficiently struck to secure Gödel an invitation to the Institute for Advanced Study in its first year of operation — the connection that would shelter Gödel through his later life. The Dictionary of Scientific Biography records that from 1932 to 1936 he published numerous short articles in these proceedings, including his only collaborative work, and co-edited seven of the volumes.

The logic and mathematics papers range more widely than their brevity suggests. Zur intuitionistischen Arithmetik und Zahlentheorie (Heft 4, pp. 34–38) is the ‘negative translation’ embedding classical arithmetic within intuitionist arithmetic and so proving the two equiconsistent — a result Gentzen and Bernays reached independently and slightly later, and one that gives the classical mathematician an intuitionistic consistency proof for ordinary arithmetic. In answer to a direct question from Hahn, Über Unabhängigkeitsbeweise im Aussagenkalkül (Heft 4) showed that not every independence proof in the propositional calculus can be carried out with finite many-valued truth tables; in answer to one from Menger, another Heft 3 note showed that any realisation of the propositional axioms partitions into classes behaving like the true and the false. Gödel’s contributions to geometry, long overlooked, run alongside the logic: two papers of February 1932 answer questions raised at earlier sessions — one showing that any quadruple of points isometric to four non-coplanar points of ordinary space can be placed, under the geodesic metric, on the surface of a sphere; the other recasting Wald’s axioms for the betweenness relation as a theorem about triples of real numbers. There is a note proving that every line-preserving one-to-one map of the real projective plane is a collineation, and Gödel’s only joint publication, a discussion of coordinate-free differential geometry written with Menger and Abraham Wald (Heft 5), bearing on Menger’s programme to characterise Gaussian surfaces without coordinates. Heft 7 carries two further items long overlooked by bibliographers: a remark following Wald, and Über die Länge von Beweisen (pp. 23–24), a brief but genuinely original proof-theory note — that passing to a stronger system can shorten proofs without limit — now read as an ancestor of the speed-up theorems of computational complexity.

The three final Hefte turned the colloquium, almost incidentally, into the birthplace of mathematical general-equilibrium theory. At the session of 19 March 1934 the banker and economist Karl Schlesinger posed a question aimed at the heart of Walrasian theory, proposing the modification of Léon Walras’s and Gustav Cassel’s production equations — that the price of a factor available in free supply must fall to zero — that made the problem tractable (Über die Produktionsgleichungen der ökonomischen Wertlehre, Heft 6, pp. 10–11). The point was not idle: economists had long supposed that a market system was determinate so long as it offered as many equations as unknowns, but counting equations guarantees neither that a solution exists nor that its prices and quantities come out non-negative, as any economic solution must. At that same meeting Abraham Wald proved that the reformulated system does have a solution, and at the session of 6 November 1934 established existence under far weaker conditions; his two papers (Heft 6, pp. 12–18, and Heft 7, pp. 1–6) were the first rigorous existence proofs for a general competitive equilibrium, and Wald himself the bridge from Walras’s nineteenth-century system to the work of Arrow, Debreu and McKenzie two decades later. Von Neumann closed the sequence with Über ein ökonomisches Gleichungssystem und eine Verallgemeinerung des Brouwerschen Fixpunktsatzes (Heft 8, pp. 73–83), the last article in the final Heft — a paper he had first sketched at Princeton in the early 1930s, presented to Menger’s colloquium in Vienna in 1936, and saw into print the following year. His expanding-economy model has two parts: a linear input–output system in which production may be circular — one good made with the help of another, and that other with the help of the first — and which grows at a uniform rate, and a generalisation of Brouwer’s fixed-point theorem, carrying a minimax argument, that proves an equilibrium exists. From it von Neumann drew the striking conclusion that, in such an economy, the maximal rate of expansion must equal the rate of interest — the result that survives in growth theory as the von Neumann model and its balanced-growth ray. It was the first application of a topological fixed-point theorem to economic equilibrium and the direct forerunner of linear programming and activity analysis. The fates of the three authors trace the same political collapse that thinned the late Hefte: Schlesinger took his own life at the Anschluss of March 1938, Wald emigrated to the United States, where he founded statistical decision theory before dying in an air crash in 1950, and von Neumann, already at Princeton, would carry the line forward to the Theory of Games and Economic Behavior with Oskar Morgenstern in 1944.

The von Neumann paper’s passage from neglect to celebrity is itself instructive. Richard Goodwin recalled that Schumpeter asked him about 1938 to report on it for a seminar, that he ‘rashly judged it to be totally unrealistic’, and that he later counted the dismissal his greatest single intellectual mistake, having failed to see in what he took for mere ingenuity one of the great formative works of the century — an oversight he believed had cost the paper its place in Schumpeter’s own monumental History of Economic Analysis. Rediscovered through its English translation, A Model of General Economic Equilibrium (Review of Economic Studies, 1945–46), the paper became a touchstone: E. Roy Weintraub, then president of the History of Economics Society, called it ‘the greatest paper in mathematical economics that was ever written’ (quoted in Cabral, 2003). In the foreword he contributed to the colloquium’s 1998 facsimile reprint, the Nobel laureate Gerard Debreu judged that the seminar’s eight years had a lasting influence on economic theory far beyond what its brevity would suggest, dated the decisive transformation of the field to Schlesinger’s question of March 1934, and held that Wald’s two existence proofs marked a turning point in the discipline. The New Palgrave reckons that von Neumann’s influence will persist in economics for centuries. The level of mathematical sophistication this Vienna sequence demanded — systems of inequalities and fixed-point arguments where economists had been content to count equations against unknowns — is much of the reason the modern subject is now written by applied mathematicians. Karl Sigmund, who edited the colloquium’s reprint and has written its history in Exact Thinking in Demented Times (2017), places the seminar at the centre of a Viennese intellectual world that produced foundational work in logic, economics and topology in the same years it was being dismantled by the politics around it.

Rarity attends the set unevenly. The first five Hefte, issued through Teubner between 1931 and 1933, are uncommon but obtainable; the last three, the Deuticke issues of 1934 to 1937, are markedly scarcer, and were probably printed in much smaller numbers amid the political turmoil that began with the failed Nazi putsch of July 1934 and the unravelling of Menger’s circle — Hefte 7 and 8 each appeared a full year behind the colloquium’s established November schedule. The consequence is plain in the market: no complete run of all eight has been traced through any of the major auction houses across the last fifteen years, the work passing instead through the hands of specialist dealers, while what does reach the salerooms is partial — a run of the first five, or of six wanting the final Heft. Individual numbers, the Gödel Heft 3 or a stray early part, surface far more often, and for a small fraction of a complete set’s value; the celebrated papers — the incompleteness recast, the equilibrium model — are usually met detached from the run that gave them their setting. These were fragile things to begin with, thin pamphlets in soft printed wrappers, prone to spine splits, chipping and loss, and a set carried intact across nine decades is the exception rather than the rule. Assembling all eight, across two publishers and including the late Deuticke parts, is the labour of years; the 1998 Springer facsimile, edited by Egbert Dierker and Karl Sigmund with the Debreu foreword and Dawson’s account of the logical contributions, has since made the texts accessible to readers but is no substitute for the originals.

From this one seminar two lineages run forward. Gödel’s arithmetisation of syntax — the coding of formulae and proofs as natural numbers — passed through his 1934 Princeton lectures into the recursive-function theory on which Alonzo Church and Alan Turing built their 1936 analyses of computation, and so into the theory of the computer itself. The linear input–output structure of von Neumann’s model became, in other hands, the activity analysis of Koopmans and the linear programming of Kantorovich and Dantzig; the equilibrium thread passed, by way of game theory and the minimax theorem, into the existence proof that Kenneth Arrow and Gerard Debreu published in Econometrica in 1954 and into Debreu’s Theory of Value (1959), the axiomatic summa of general-equilibrium economics. That a single colloquium, meeting on alternate Tuesdays in a city about to destroy its own intellectual life, should have seeded both the logic of the undecidable and the mathematics of the market is the fact these eight pamphlets record. The two lines ran through the same small group in the same few years — a group soon scattered across the Atlantic or dead — and only a complete run of all eight Hefte holds them together as the single object they once were: the printed memory of two revolutions that shared one room.

Physical description

Eight separate issues (Hefte 1–8), 8vo (232 × 152 mm). Collation: pp. 31, [1, blank]; 38, [2, blank]; 26; 45, [1, blank]; 42; 47, [1, blank]; 61, [1, blank]; 84. Hefte 1–5 in the Teubner imprint, the last three issued by Deuticke. Original printed wrappers throughout. Heft 2 with a small repair to the spine; Heft 7 neatly rebacked; Heft 8 with the wrappers chipped at the edges and the spine strengthened with Japanese tissue; light foxing and spotting to the wrappers, somewhat heavier on a few. All parts internally near fine.
